text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Tuesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- Volvo's new model, the C70, is designed to attract customers who care more about image than price.
- Heads of Swedish companies tend to travel more than their counterparts from other European countries, on average 60 hours per month, survey shows.
- Abuse of the state welfare system is on the rise.
- Chicago-based Morton International, whose automotive safety unit is to merge with Sweden's Autoliv, is twice as big as Autoliv and is a leader in its markets.
Analysts welcomed the merger, saying their geographical positions will open new markets for both firms.

- An international report shows Sweden is an attractive place for money laundering, especially from Russia and eastern Europe, partly because its banking system so modern that there is little face-to-face contact with customers.

- Vehicle airbag maker Autoliv's former managing director Gunnar Bark will make a comeback in the new company formed through the merger of Autoliv and the automotive unit of U.S.-based Morton, becoming chairman of the new firm's board.

- Shares in steel firms SSAB and Avesta Sheffield rose after a forecast announced at the annual meeting of the International Iron and Steel Institute in Helsinki indicating steel consumption would reach a record 680 million tonnes in 1997.
